Mede a glicose a cada 5 minutos, sem precisar furar o dedo o tempo todo;

[PAGE 1]

Mostra tendências com setas (se a glicose está subindo ou caindo);

[PAGE 1]

Pode disparar alarmes antes de a glicose cair demais;

[PAGE 1]

Ajuda a ver como a glicose se comporta durante a madrugada, quando ninguém está medindo com glicosímetro;

[PAGE 1]

Estudos mostram que ajuda a diminuir a hemoglobina glicada (HbA1c) e os episódios de hipoglicemia.

[PAGE 1]

🧠 Importante saber: o que é o “lag time”?

[PAGE 1]

Existe uma diferença de tempo entre a glicemia medida no sensor e no sangue do dedo.
 Essa diferença é de mais ou menos 10 minutos.

[PAGE 1]

 Se o sensor mostra 76 mg/dL com seta para baixo, pode ser que a glicemia real já esteja em 50 mg/dL.

[PAGE 1]

Outros funcionam sozinhos, como:

[PAGE 1]

FreeStyle Libre® (muito usado no Brasil);

[PAGE 1]

Dexcom® (ainda não disponível no Brasil).

[PAGE 1]

Calibração:

[PAGE 1]

Alguns sensores precisam ser calibrados com furinho no dedo (glicemia capilar), geralmente em jejum ou antes das refeições.

[PAGE 1]

O FreeStyle Libre® não precisa de calibração e funciona por 14 dias direto.

[PAGE 1]

[PAGE 1]

Mesmo assim, usar o sensor com frequência ajuda muito a controlar o diabetes e reduzir a HbA1c.

[PAGE 1]

[PAGE 1]

Antigamente, os sensores eram só para acompanhar, e ainda era necessário confirmar com o glicosímetro antes de aplicar insulina.

[PAGE 1]

Mas isso mudou!

[PAGE 1]

[PAGE 1]

O estudo REPLACE-BG mostrou que isso é seguro e eficaz para adultos com DM1 que estão bem controlados.

[PAGE 1]

✅ Conclusão: por que o CGM é tão importante?

[PAGE 1]

O sensor de glicose:

[PAGE 1]

Facilita muito o controle do diabetes;

[PAGE 1]

Evita crises de hipoglicemia ou hiperglicemia;

[PAGE 1]

Ajuda a você e seu médico ajustarem melhor o tratamento;

[PAGE 1]

Pode substituir o uso frequente do glicosímetro em muitos casos.

[PAGE 1]

Se você tem diabetes tipo 1, hipoglicemias frequentes ou está usando insulina várias vezes ao dia, vale conversar com seu médico sobre o uso de um sensor.

Banting was a Canadian physician and medical researcher renowned for his central role in the discovery and development of insulin, a transformative treatment for diabetes. Working at the University of Toronto, Banting secured a lecturer position that provided the foundation for his research, where he collaborated closely with Charles Best. Together, they conducted pioneering experiments on pancreatic extracts, initially termed "Isletin," focusing on isolating the substance responsible for regulating blood sugar. A pivotal moment in their research came through experiments on diabetic dogs, particularly Dog #92, which exhibited remarkable recovery after receiving the pancreatic extract. This breakthrough demonstrated the extract’s efficacy and laid the experimental groundwork for insulin therapy.

Banting’s contributions extended beyond the laboratory into direct clinical application. He was one of the lead researchers in the first human trials of insulin and played an active role in patient selection and treatment. He administered insulin to several early patients, including Elizabeth Hughes, daughter of U.S. Secretary of State Charles Evans Hughes, and closely monitored the recovery of Elsie Needham from a diabetic coma. Banting also admitted Charlotte Clarke as a candidate for insulin therapy, underscoring his involvement in patient care during the experimental phase. Demonstrating personal commitment to the therapy’s safety, Banting tested the pancreatic extract on himself before human trials. He further marked a significant milestone by delivering the first dose of insulin in the United States to Jim Havens, a young patient with severe diabetes.

In addition to his experimental and clinical work, Banting was instrumental in disseminating the discovery to the medical community. He presented the team’s findings at medical conventions, accelerating the global recognition and adoption of insulin therapy. Although initially reluctant to seek personal recognition, Banting ultimately agreed to have his name included on the patent for insulin, a formal acknowledgment of his indispensable role. His leadership, dedication, and hands-on approach—from laboratory research to patient treatment—were central to one of the most significant medical advancements of the 20th century.

Insulin is a hormone produced by the beta cells of the pancreas, specifically within the islets of Langerhans, and plays a central role in regulating blood glucose levels and carbohydrate metabolism. It facilitates the uptake of glucose from the bloodstream into cells for energy production, making it essential for normal metabolic function. Insulin was discovered in 1921 through groundbreaking research conducted at the University of Toronto by Frederick Banting, Charles Best, James Collip, and John Macleod, under the initial guidance and support of Macleod. Originally referred to as "Isletin," the name was derived from the Latin term for "island," referencing the islets of Langerhans where the hormone is synthesized. This discovery marked a pivotal medical breakthrough, transforming diabetes mellitus—a previously fatal condition—into a manageable disease.

As a therapeutic agent, insulin is used to treat diabetes mellitus, a chronic disorder characterized by the body’s inability to produce sufficient insulin (type 1 diabetes) or to use it effectively (type 2 diabetes). It enables individuals with diabetes to achieve glycemic control, thereby reducing the risk of long-term complications such as neuropathy, retinopathy, and cardiovascular disease. Insulin is administered via subcutaneous injection or through continuous delivery systems like insulin pumps, with dosing measured in international units. Due to the serious risks of hypoglycemia or hyperglycemia from incorrect dosing, insulin is classified as a high-alert medication. Various formulations exist to meet diverse metabolic needs, including rapid-acting, short-acting, intermediate-acting (e.g., NPH), and long-acting analogs, each differing in onset, peak, and duration of action.

Proper administration of insulin involves selecting appropriate injection sites—typically areas with adequate subcutaneous fat—and rotating these sites regularly to prevent complications such as lipodystrophy, infection, or impaired absorption. The hormone must be stored and transported within specific temperature ranges, as exposure to extreme heat, cold, or direct sunlight can degrade its potency. Patients require comprehensive education on storage, hygiene, accurate dosing, and safe disposal of needles and delivery devices. Dosage requirements may vary over time due to changes in health status, weight, or lifestyle, necessitating ongoing monitoring and individualized adjustments to maintain optimal therapeutic outcomes.

        *   `entity_type`: Categorize the entity using one of the following types: `Person,Creature,Organization,Location,Event,Concept,Method,Content,Data,Artifact,NaturalObject`. If none of the provided entity types apply, do not add new entity type and classify it as `Other`.

    *   **Output Format - Entities:** Output a total of 4 fields for each entity, delimited by `<|#|>`, on a single line. The first field *must* be the literal string `entity`.
        *   Format: `entity<|#|>entity_name<|#|>entity_type<|#|>entity_description`

2.  **Relationship Extraction & Output:**
    *   **Identification:** Identify direct, clearly stated, and meaningful relationships between previously extracted entities.
    *   **N-ary Relationship Decomposition:** If a single statement describes a relationship involving more than two entities (an N-ary relationship), decompose it into multiple binary (two-entity) relationship pairs for separate description.
        *   **Example:** For "Alice, Bob, and Carol collaborated on Project X," extract binary relationships such as "Alice collaborated with Project X," "Bob collaborated with Project X," and "Carol collaborated with Project X," or "Alice collaborated with Bob," based on the most reasonable binary interpretations.
    *   **Relationship Details:** For each binary relationship, extract the following fields:
        *   `source_entity`: The name of the source entity. Ensure **consistent naming** with entity extraction. Capitalize the first letter of each significant word (title case) if the name is case-insensitive.
        *   `target_entity`: The name of the target entity. Ensure **consistent naming** with entity extraction. Capitalize the first letter of each significant word (title case) if the name is case-insensitive.
        *   `relationship_keywords`: One or more high-level keywords summarizing the overarching nature, concepts, or themes of the relationship. Multiple keywords within this field must be separated by a comma `,`. **DO NOT use `<|#|>` for separating multiple keywords within this field.**
        *   `relationship_description`: A concise explanation of the nature of the relationship between the source and target entities, providing a clear rationale for their connection.
    *   **Output Format - Relationships:** Output a total of 5 fields for each relationship, delimited by `<|#|>`, on a single line. The first field *must* be the literal string `relation`.
        *   Format: `relation<|#|>source_entity<|#|>target_entity<|#|>relationship_keywords<|#|>relationship_description`

3.  **Delimiter Usage Protocol:**
    *   The `<|#|>` is a complete, atomic marker and **must not be filled with content**. It serves strictly as a field separator.

    *   **Correct Example:** `entity<|#|>Tokyo<|#|>location<|#|>Tokyo is the capital of Japan.`

4.  **Relationship Direction & Duplication:**
    *   Treat all relationships as **undirected** unless explicitly stated otherwise. Swapping the source and target entities for an undirected relationship does not constitute a new relationship.
    *   Avoid outputting duplicate relationships.

5.  **Output Order & Prioritization:**
    *   Output all extracted entities first, followed by all extracted relationships.
    *   Within the list of relationships, prioritize and output those relationships that are **most significant** to the core meaning of the input text first.

6.  **Context & Objectivity:**
    *   Ensure all entity names and descriptions are written in the **third person**.
    *   Explicitly name the subject or object; **avoid using pronouns** such as `this article`, `this paper`, `our company`, `I`, `you`, and `he/she`.

7.  **Language & Proper Nouns:**
    *   The entire output (entity names, keywords, and descriptions) must be written in `English`.
    *   Proper nouns (e.g., personal names, place names, organization names) should be retained in their original language if a proper, widely accepted translation is not available or would cause ambiguity.

Multiple factors contribute to the development of hypoglycemia. In insulin-treated patients, these include incorrect dosing, improper injection techniques—such as intramuscular delivery due to long needles or injection into areas with lipo-hypertrophy—and inadequate site rotation, all of which disrupt the expected pharmacokinetics of insulin absorption. External factors like exercise, heat, and massage can accelerate insulin uptake, increasing the risk of sudden glucose drops, particularly when insulin is administered before physical activity. The risk varies by insulin type and delivery method; long- and ultra-long-acting insulin analogs are associated with a reduced incidence of hypoglycemia, and insulin pump therapy, especially in children and adolescents, has been shown to lower event frequency compared to traditional syringes.

Prevention and management of hypoglycemia rely heavily on patient education, proper injection practices, and technological interventions. Regular blood glucose monitoring is essential for prevention, and continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) systems play a critical role by providing real-time data, trend analysis, and early warning alarms for declining glucose levels. CGM use has been particularly effective in reducing hypoglycemic episodes in type 1 diabetes. Advanced systems, including hybrid closed-loop insulin delivery devices, can automatically adjust insulin dosing in response to low glucose, further enhancing safety. Rapid-acting insulin analogs also contribute to improved glycemic control with a lower hypoglycemia risk. The effectiveness of insulin delivery methods plays a critical role in preventing DKA, underscoring the importance of reliable and consistent insulin administration.

Treatment typically involves insulin therapy, often administered via intravenous infusion, to restore metabolic balance and reverse the acidotic state. Macleod is a professor and senior researcher at the University of Toronto who played a central and multifaceted role in the discovery and development of insulin. As a supervisory figure in the landmark diabetes research project, he provided essential laboratory space and resources to Frederick Banting and Charles Best, arranged retroactive pay for Banting, and offered consistent scientific guidance throughout their experiments on pancreatic extracts. His leadership was characterized by a cautious and rigorous approach, as he repeatedly urged Banting and Best to validate their findings and focus on confirming the therapeutic effectiveness of their results. Banting frequently communicated with Macleod, reporting progress and awaiting instructions, underscoring Macleod’s authoritative and mentorship role in the research endeavor.

Macleod expanded the research team by inviting biochemist James Collip to join, ensuring the scientific and biochemical integrity of the work. He was a co-author of the seminal paper published in the Canadian Medical Association Journal, which detailed the discovery and medical potential of insulin, cementing his status as an integral member of the Toronto research team. During a presentation in Washington, D.C., Macleod named the pancreatic extract "insulin," a term that became universally adopted. His name was initially linked to the serum used in the first successful human treatment of Leonard Thompson, reflecting his perceived leadership in the project. Additionally, Macleod participated in pivotal decisions regarding the patenting and ethical dissemination of insulin, helping shape the framework for its scientific and public accessibility.

This article marked the beginning of widespread media coverage on the medical breakthrough and brought public attention to the research being conducted by doctors in Toronto.

HbA1c, or glycated hemoglobin, is a clinical biomarker that reflects the average blood glucose levels over the past two to three months by measuring the percentage of hemoglobin in red blood cells that has become glycated. It serves as a key indicator of long-term glycemic control in individuals with diabetes and is widely used in clinical practice to evaluate the effectiveness of diabetes management strategies, including insulin therapies, lifestyle interventions, and patient education programs. The test is frequently employed as a primary endpoint in clinical studies assessing the efficacy of treatments such as insulin pump therapy or continuous subcutaneous insulin infusion (CSII), which has been shown to improve HbA1c outcomes compared to multiple daily injections (MDI) in some cases. Structured diabetes education has also been demonstrated to significantly reduce HbA1c levels, highlighting the role of patient engagement in achieving better glucose management.

HbA1c is used as a benchmark in diabetes care and correlates with time in range (TIR), a metric derived from continuous glucose monitoring (CGM). Studies consistently show that CGM use is associated with lower HbA1c levels, reinforcing its value in optimizing glycemic control. The biomarker is also instrumental in guiding treatment decisions for high-risk populations, particularly pregnant women with diabetes. Clinical guidelines recommend an HbA1c target below 6.5% for women planning pregnancy or in the first trimester, with a stricter goal of below 6.0% during the second and third trimesters to minimize maternal and fetal risks. These targets underscore the importance of tight glucose control at critical stages of care.

Across various treatment regimens, HbA1c remains a reliable measure for comparing therapeutic efficacy. For example, insulin lispro and regular human insulin have been shown to achieve comparable HbA1c levels in pediatric populations, indicating that different insulin formulations can support equivalent glycemic control. As a standardized blood test measuring average plasma glucose over time, HbA1c continues to be a cornerstone in both clinical management and research, providing a consistent and objective assessment of long-term diabetes control.

[PAGE 1]

🩸 Entendendo o Diabetes e o Controle da Glicose

[PAGE 1]

🤔 O que é o diabetes?

[PAGE 1]

O diabetes mellitus (DM) é uma doença que acontece quando o corpo não consegue produzir ou usar a insulina corretamente. A insulina é o hormônio que ajuda o açúcar (glicose) a entrar nas células e virar energia.

[PAGE 1]

Existem dois tipos principais de diabetes:

[PAGE 1]

Diabetes tipo 1 (DM1): o corpo para de produzir insulina porque o sistema de defesa (imunidade) ataca as células do pâncreas que fazem insulina.

[PAGE 1]

Diabetes tipo 2 (DM2): o corpo até produz insulina, mas ela não funciona bem (isso se chama resistência à insulina) e, com o tempo, a produção também vai diminuindo.

[PAGE 1]

⚠️ Por que é importante controlar o açúcar no sangue?

[PAGE 1]

Se o açúcar no sangue fica muito alto ou muito baixo, o corpo sofre. Quando isso acontece com frequência, pode causar complicações graves, como:

[PAGE 1]

Problemas nos olhos (retinopatia)

[PAGE 1]

Problemas nos rins

[PAGE 1]

Dores e perda de sensibilidade nas mãos e pés (neuropatia)

[PAGE 1]

Infartos e derrames

[PAGE 1]

Esses problemas podem diminuir a qualidade de vida, aumentar o risco de morte precoce e gerar custos altos com tratamentos.

[PAGE 1]

🔬 O que a “disglicemia” faz no corpo?

[PAGE 1]

“Disglicemia” é quando o açúcar no sangue não está equilibrado, ou seja, nem sempre alto, nem sempre baixo — mas oscilando bastante.

[PAGE 1]

Essas oscilações prejudicam muitas partes do corpo:

[PAGE 1]

Causam inflamações internas;

[PAGE 1]

Danificam os vasos sanguíneos;

[PAGE 1]

Podem mudar a forma como algumas células funcionam, inclusive do sistema de defesa;

[PAGE 1]

Contribuem para o que os médicos chamam de “memória metabólica” — é como se o corpo "guardasse" os efeitos ruins do açúcar alto, mesmo depois de melhorar o controle.

[PAGE 1]

🎯 Qual é o objetivo do tratamento?

[PAGE 1]

O principal objetivo do tratamento do diabetes é evitar essas complicações, mantendo o açúcar no sangue dentro de valores seguros. Para isso, os médicos observam algumas metas, como:

[PAGE 1]

Glicemia de jejum (antes de comer);

[PAGE 1]

Glicemia após as refeições;

[PAGE 1]

Hemoglobina glicada (HbA1c) — que mostra a média do açúcar dos últimos 2 a 3 meses.

[PAGE 1]

📈 Como o controle do açúcar foi medido ao longo do tempo?

[PAGE 1]

🕰️ Uma breve história dos testes de glicemia

[PAGE 1]

1921: a insulina foi descoberta e testada em cães. Pouco depois, começou a ser usada em pessoas.

[PAGE 1]

1925: os testes de urina começaram a ser usados em casa para saber se havia açúcar no xixi.

[PAGE 1]

1964: surgiu o primeiro teste para medir o açúcar no sangue a partir de uma gota de sangue do dedo — era o começo dos monitores de glicemia.

[PAGE 1]

Desde então, os exames melhoraram muito! Hoje temos:

[PAGE 1]

HbA1c: mostra a média da glicemia dos últimos 3 meses;

[PAGE 1]

AMGC: a pessoa faz pequenos furos no dedo e mede o açúcar com um aparelhinho (automonitoramento da glicemia capilar);

[PAGE 1]

Monitoramento contínuo de glicose (SMCG): sensores que ficam colados na pele e medem a glicose a cada poucos minutos;

[PAGE 1]

Sensor “flash” de glicose: parecido com o SMCG, mas a pessoa precisa passar o leitor no sensor para ver os dados.

[PAGE 1]

Além disso, estão sendo criados novos sensores, como:

[PAGE 1]

Medidores que funcionam como um relógio ou uma lente de contato;

[PAGE 1]

Medidores que usam luz ou calor, sem precisar furar o dedo;

[PAGE 1]

Sensores colocados como uma tatuagem, que mostram a glicose pela pele.

[PAGE 1]

🩸 Hemoglobina glicada (HbA1c): o exame principal

[PAGE 1]

A HbA1c é um exame de sangue que mostra a média do açúcar dos últimos 2 ou 3 meses.

[PAGE 1]

📌 Quanto mais alto o resultado, mais açúcar estava circulando no seu sangue nesse período.

[PAGE 1]

Por que é importante?

[PAGE 1]

Estudos mostraram que quanto mais alta a HbA1c, maiores os riscos de complicações, como:

[PAGE 1]

Doença nos olhos, rins e nervos;

[PAGE 1]

Doenças do coração e vasos.

[PAGE 1]

Por isso, baixar a HbA1c é um dos principais objetivos do tratamento.

[PAGE 1]

😕 Mas a HbA1c tem algumas limitações

[PAGE 1]

Ela não mostra os picos de glicemia (subidas e descidas rápidas).

[PAGE 1]

Não mostra se a pessoa tem hipoglicemias frequentes.

🤔 O que é o diabetes?

[PAGE 1]

O diabetes mellitus (DM) é uma doença que acontece quando o corpo não consegue produzir ou usar a insulina corretamente. A insulina é o hormônio que ajuda o açúcar (glicose) a entrar nas células e virar energia.

[PAGE 1]

Existem dois tipos principais de diabetes:

[PAGE 1]

[PAGE 1]

⚠️ Por que é importante controlar o açúcar no sangue?

[PAGE 1]

Se o açúcar no sangue fica muito alto ou muito baixo, o corpo sofre. Quando isso acontece com frequência, pode causar complicações graves, como:

[PAGE 1]

Problemas nos olhos (retinopatia)

Problemas nos rins

Dores e perda de sensibilidade nas mãos e pés (neuropatia)

[PAGE 1]

“Disglicemia” é quando o açúcar no sangue não está equilibrado, ou seja, nem sempre alto, nem sempre baixo — mas oscilando bastante.

[PAGE 1]

Essas oscilações prejudicam muitas partes do corpo:

Causam inflamações internas;

Danificam os vasos sanguíneos;

🎯 Qual é o objetivo do tratamento?

[PAGE 1]

O principal objetivo do tratamento do diabetes é evitar essas complicações, mantendo o açúcar no sangue dentro de valores seguros. Para isso, os médicos observam algumas metas, como:

Glicemia de jejum (antes de comer);

Glicemia após as refeições;

1925: os testes de urina começaram a ser usados em casa para saber se havia açúcar no xixi.

The pancreas is an organ in the human body that plays a critical role in regulating blood glucose levels through the production of insulin. It is primarily responsible for synthesizing and secreting insulin, a hormone essential for enabling cells to absorb glucose from the bloodstream for energy. This function places the pancreas at the center of metabolic regulation and makes it a key focus in the study of diabetes and other metabolic disorders.

The importance of the pancreas has been historically demonstrated through research involving its removal and the analysis of its internal secretions, which were pivotal in uncovering the metabolic effects of insulin. These studies laid the foundation for understanding how insulin functions and how its absence or deficiency leads to disease. In particular, the pancreas is directly involved in type 1 diabetes, an autoimmune condition in which the body's immune system attacks and destroys the insulin-producing beta cells within the organ. As a result, individuals with type 1 diabetes are unable to produce sufficient insulin, necessitating external insulin administration to maintain glucose homeostasis.

Insulin is a hormone produced by the beta cells of the pancreas, specifically within the islets of Langerhans, and plays a central role in regulating blood glucose levels and carbohydrate metabolism. It enables glucose to enter cells, where it is converted into energy, making insulin essential for normal metabolic function. The hormone was originally referred to as "Isletin," a name derived from the Latin term for "island," referencing the islets of Langerhans where it is synthesized. This discovery was the result of groundbreaking research conducted at the University of Toronto in 1921 by Frederick Banting, Charles Best, James Collip, and John Macleod, with Macleod providing initial guidance and support. The identification of insulin marked a pivotal medical breakthrough, transforming diabetes mellitus—a previously fatal condition—into a manageable disease.

As a therapeutic agent, insulin is used to treat diabetes mellitus, a chronic disorder characterized by the body’s inability to produce sufficient insulin (type 1 diabetes) or to use it effectively (type 2 diabetes). It is administered via subcutaneous injection or through continuous delivery systems such as insulin pumps, with dosing measured in international units. Various formulations exist to meet diverse metabolic needs, including rapid-acting, short-acting, intermediate-acting (e.g., NPH), and long-acting analogs, each differing in onset, peak, and duration of action. Due to the serious risks of hypoglycemia or hyperglycemia from incorrect dosing, insulin is classified as a high-alert medication.

Proper administration requires selecting appropriate injection sites—typically areas with adequate subcutaneous fat—and rotating these sites regularly to prevent complications such as lipodystrophy, infection, or impaired absorption. Insulin must be stored and transported within specific temperature ranges, as exposure to extreme heat, cold, or direct sunlight can degrade its potency. Patients require comprehensive education on storage, hygiene, accurate dosing, and safe disposal of needles and delivery devices. Dosage requirements may vary over time due to changes in health status, weight, or lifestyle, necessitating ongoing monitoring and individualized adjustments to maintain optimal glycemic control and reduce the risk of long-term complications such as neuropathy, retinopathy, and cardiovascular disease.

It is a key concern in diabetes management and is typically detectable using a glucometer, which measures blood glucose levels for diagnosis and ongoing monitoring. The condition arises primarily from disruptions in insulin function, particularly in individuals with diabetes who depend on insulin therapy for glucose regulation. Elevated glucose levels can occur postprandially and are a primary target for glucose control in therapeutic strategies. If left unmanaged, hyperglycemia can lead to serious health issues, including acute and chronic complications associated with diabetes, contributing to long-term complications such as neuropathy, retinopathy, and cardiovascular disease, as well as increased risks of hospitalization.

Several factors contribute to the development of hyperglycemia in diabetic patients. A significant cause is improper insulin absorption, often due to complications at injection sites, such as lipo-hypertrophy—fatty tissue buildup resulting from repeated insulin injections in the same location. When insulin is administered into these affected areas, its absorption becomes erratic or incomplete, leading to insufficient cellular glucose uptake and sustained high blood glucose levels. This issue is exacerbated by poor injection practices, including the reuse of pen needles, which can cause insulin leakage and reduced delivery efficiency. Documented cases, particularly in pediatric patients, have shown hyperglycemia resulting directly from such technical errors in insulin administration.

Additionally, in individuals using continuous subcutaneous insulin infusion (CSII) or insulin pump therapy, hyperglycemia can occur due to infusion site failure, disconnection, or pump malfunction, which interrupt insulin delivery. Despite these risks, insulin pump therapy is also recognized as a method that can improve postprandial glucose management when functioning correctly. Effective prevention and management of hyperglycemia require vigilant blood glucose monitoring, proper insulin administration techniques, regular rotation of injection or infusion sites, and timely intervention in response to device-related issues. Overall, hyperglycemia remains a critical challenge in diabetes care, necessitating comprehensive patient education and adherence to best practices to mitigate associated health risks.

O que é Glicemia Capilar?

[PAGE 3]

A glicemia capilar é uma técnica de aferição rápida a partir de uma gota de sangue que verifica a concentração de glicose nos vasos capilares da polpa digital de uma das extremidades do corpo, por meio de um aparelho chamado glicosímetro que utiliza tiras biossensoras descartáveis contendo glicose desidrogenase ou glicose oxidase acoplada a um dispositivo que faz a captação elétrica da hemoglobina(1-2).

[PAGE 3]

Terminologia para a glicemia capilar

[PAGE 3]

Um termo ainda muito utilizado para se referir à glicemia capilar é o “dextro”. O Dextrostix foi a primeira tira para medição de glicemia capilar desenvolvida em 1965, e que se popularizou amplamente nas décadas subsequentes. A partir de 1990, outras tiras e leitores de glicose, alguns já usando tecnologias diferentes foram criados e o Dextrostix aos poucos deixou de ser usado(3-4). Dessa forma, “dextro” é a abreviação do nome comercial de um produto já não disponível e que não deve ser mais utilizado. A recomendação atual na prática clínica é a utilização do termo "glicemia capilar". Outro termo comumente utilizado é o exame de ''ponta de dedo”.

[PAGE 3]

Fundamentação para a Glicemia Capilar

[PAGE 3]

Para o diagnóstico do diabetes mellitus (DM) na pessoa assintomática, não é recomendado utilizar a glicemia capilar como critério e, sim o exame de glicemia plasmática de jejum, a glicemia duas horas após uma sobrecarga de 75 g de glicose ou o exame de hemoglobina glicada (HbA1c), sendo necessário que dois exames estejam alterados. Na presença de sintomas inequívocos de hiperglicemia, é recomendado que o diagnóstico seja realizado por meio da glicemia capilar ao acaso com resultado ≥ 200 mg/dl(5).

O que é Glicemia Capilar?

[PAGE 3]

A glicemia capilar é uma técnica de aferição rápida a partir de uma gota de sangue que verifica a concentração de glicose nos vasos capilares da polpa digital de uma das extremidades do corpo, por meio de um aparelho chamado glicosímetro que utiliza tiras biossensoras descartáveis contendo glicose desidrogenase ou glicose oxidase acoplada a um dispositivo que faz a captação elétrica da hemoglobina(1-2).

[PAGE 3]

Terminologia para a glicemia capilar

[PAGE 3]

Um termo ainda muito utilizado para se referir à glicemia capilar é o “dextro”. O Dextrostix foi a primeira tira para medição de glicemia capilar desenvolvida em 1965, e que se popularizou amplamente nas décadas subsequentes. A partir de 1990, outras tiras e leitores de glicose, alguns já usando tecnologias diferentes foram criados e o Dextrostix aos poucos deixou de ser usado(3-4). Dessa forma, “dextro” é a abreviação do nome comercial de um produto já não disponível e que não deve ser mais utilizado. A recomendação atual na prática clínica é a utilização do termo "glicemia capilar". Outro termo comumente utilizado é o exame de ''ponta de dedo”.

[PAGE 3]

Fundamentação para a Glicemia Capilar

[PAGE 3]

Para o diagnóstico do diabetes mellitus (DM) na pessoa assintomática, não é recomendado utilizar a glicemia capilar como critério e, sim o exame de glicemia plasmática de jejum, a glicemia duas horas após uma sobrecarga de 75 g de glicose ou o exame de hemoglobina glicada (HbA1c), sendo necessário que dois exames estejam alterados. Na presença de sintomas inequívocos de hiperglicemia, é recomendado que o diagnóstico seja realizado por meio da glicemia capilar ao acaso com resultado ≥ 200 mg/dl(5).

[PAGE 3]

O monitoramento diário da glicemia capilar é a base do manejo para o controle intensivo do diabetes e está associado ao controle glicêmico para prevenção de complicações agudas e crônicas.

Glicemia Capilar refers to the measurement of blood glucose levels using capillary blood, typically obtained through a finger prick. This method involves collecting a small drop of blood from the fingertip, which is then analyzed using a glucometer equipped with disposable biosensor strips, providing a rapid assessment of glucose levels. It is commonly described in clinical settings as "poking the finger" or "doing a little prick" and is a traditional approach to glucose monitoring.

The test is performed at specific times, including during fasting and after meals (pre- and post-prandially), to track glucose fluctuations, particularly in individuals with diabetes. This monitoring approach is especially relevant in managing gestational diabetes, where capillary blood glucose levels are regularly assessed in pregnant women to ensure proper glycemic control. Glicemia Capilar serves as a key measure in diabetes management, allowing patients and healthcare providers to make informed decisions about treatment and lifestyle adjustments.

Data from capillary glucose measurements can be recorded in various formats, including paper diaries, spreadsheets, mobile applications, or cloud-based software, facilitating ongoing clinical follow-up. These records are often documented in patient charts or monitoring logs for longitudinal assessment. Despite its widespread use, glicemia capilar is considered less effective compared to continuous glucose monitoring in reducing both hypoglycemic events and HbA1c levels, highlighting limitations in its precision and consistency for long-term glycemic control. Nevertheless, it remains a fundamental tool in routine diabetes care due to its accessibility and ease of use.

It is widely recognized for publishing the annual "Standards of Medical Care in Diabetes," a comprehensive document that provides evidence-based recommendations for the classification, diagnosis, and treatment of diabetes. These guidelines cover a broad spectrum of clinical practices, including pharmacologic therapies, insulin use, and the integration of diabetes technologies, serving as a primary reference for healthcare providers and institutions worldwide.

A central component of the ADA's mission is optimizing diabetes management through structured clinical guidance. The organization emphasizes proper insulin therapy, including injection techniques, site rotation, and the use of advanced delivery systems such as continuous subcutaneous insulin infusion (CSII) via insulin pumps. The ADA recommends rotating injection sites systematically within anatomical regions to prevent complications like lipohypertrophy and ensure consistent insulin absorption. It supports the use of diabetes technologies, particularly for motivated individuals, including young children and adolescents, and provides guidance on their effective implementation in daily care.

Beyond insulin and technology, the ADA addresses broader aspects of diabetes care, including school safety protocols for children with diabetes and strategies for glycemic control. It has issued position statements on intensive glycemic control and its role in preventing cardiovascular events, reflecting its engagement with long-term complication prevention. The ADA also collaborates with international bodies, such as co-authoring a consensus report with the European Association for the Study of Diabetes (EASD), underscoring its role in shaping global diabetes research and policy. Through its extensive publications and clinical recommendations, the American Diabetes Association remains a cornerstone in advancing diabetes care standards and patient outcomes.

        *   `entity_name`: The name of the entity. If the entity name is case-insensitive, capitalize the first letter of each significant word (title case). Ensure **consistent naming** across the entire extraction process.
        *   `entity_type`: Categorize the entity using one of the following types: `Person,Creature,Organization,Location,Event,Concept,Method,Content,Data,Artifact,NaturalObject`. If none of the provided entity types apply, do not add new entity type and classify it as `Other`.

        *   Format: `entity<|#|>entity_name<|#|>entity_type<|#|>entity_description`

2.  **Relationship Extraction & Output:**
    *   **Identification:** Identify direct, clearly stated, and meaningful relationships between previously extracted entities.
    *   **N-ary Relationship Decomposition:** If a single statement describes a relationship involving more than two entities (an N-ary relationship), decompose it into multiple binary (two-entity) relationship pairs for separate description.

        *   `source_entity`: The name of the source entity. Ensure **consistent naming** with entity extraction. Capitalize the first letter of each significant word (title case) if the name is case-insensitive.
        *   `target_entity`: The name of the target entity. Ensure **consistent naming** with entity extraction. Capitalize the first letter of each significant word (title case) if the name is case-insensitive.
        *   `relationship_keywords`: One or more high-level keywords summarizing the overarching nature, concepts, or themes of the relationship. Multiple keywords within this field must be separated by a comma `,`. **DO NOT use `<|#|>` for separating multiple keywords within this field.**
        *   `relationship_description`: A concise explanation of the nature of the relationship between the source and target entities, providing a clear rationale for their connection.

        *   Format: `relation<|#|>source_entity<|#|>target_entity<|#|>relationship_keywords<|#|>relationship_description`

    *   **Correct Example:** `entity<|#|>Tokyo<|#|>location<|#|>Tokyo is the capital of Japan.`

    *   Treat all relationships as **undirected** unless explicitly stated otherwise. Swapping the source and target entities for an undirected relationship does not constitute a new relationship.
    *   Avoid outputting duplicate relationships.

5.  **Output Order & Prioritization:**
    *   Output all extracted entities first, followed by all extracted relationships.
    *   Within the list of relationships, prioritize and output those relationships that are **most significant** to the core meaning of the input text first.

6.  **Context & Objectivity:**
    *   Ensure all entity names and descriptions are written in the **third person**.
    *   Explicitly name the subject or object; **avoid using pronouns** such as `this article`, `this paper`, `our company`, `I`, `you`, and `he/she`.

    *   The entire output (entity names, keywords, and descriptions) must be written in `English`.

---Role---

---Instructions---
1.  **Entity Extraction & Output:**
    *   **Identification:** Identify clearly defined and meaningful entities in the input text.
    *   **Entity Details:** For each identified entity, extract the following information:
        *   `entity_name`: The name of the entity. If the entity name is case-insensitive, capitalize the first letter of each significant word (title case). Ensure **consistent naming** across the entire extraction process.
        *   `entity_type`: Categorize the entity using one of the following types: `Person,Creature,Organization,Location,Event,Concept,Method,Content,Data,Artifact,NaturalObject`. If none of the provided entity types apply, do not add new entity type and classify it as `Other`.

    *   **Output Format - Entities:** Output a total of 4 fields for each entity, delimited by `<|#|>`, on a single line. The first field *must* be the literal string `entity`.
        *   Format: `entity<|#|>entity_name<|#|>entity_type<|#|>entity_description`

2.  **Relationship Extraction & Output:**
    *   **Identification:** Identify direct, clearly stated, and meaningful relationships between previously extracted entities.
    *   **N-ary Relationship Decomposition:** If a single statement describes a relationship involving more than two entities (an N-ary relationship), decompose it into multiple binary (two-entity) relationship pairs for separate description.
        *   **Example:** For "Alice, Bob, and Carol collaborated on Project X," extract binary relationships such as "Alice collaborated with Project X," "Bob collaborated with Project X," and "Carol collaborated with Project X," or "Alice collaborated with Bob," based on the most reasonable binary interpretations.
    *   **Relationship Details:** For each binary relationship, extract the following fields:
        *   `source_entity`: The name of the source entity. Ensure **consistent naming** with entity extraction. Capitalize the first letter of each significant word (title case) if the name is case-insensitive.
        *   `target_entity`: The name of the target entity. Ensure **consistent naming** with entity extraction. Capitalize the first letter of each significant word (title case) if the name is case-insensitive.
        *   `relationship_keywords`: One or more high-level keywords summarizing the overarching nature, concepts, or themes of the relationship. Multiple keywords within this field must be separated by a comma `,`. **DO NOT use `<|#|>` for separating multiple keywords within this field.**
        *   `relationship_description`: A concise explanation of the nature of the relationship between the source and target entities, providing a clear rationale for their connection.
    *   **Output Format - Relationships:** Output a total of 5 fields for each relationship, delimited by `<|#|>`, on a single line. The first field *must* be the literal string `relation`.
        *   Format: `relation<|#|>source_entity<|#|>target_entity<|#|>relationship_keywords<|#|>relationship_description`

3.  **Delimiter Usage Protocol:**
    *   The `<|#|>` is a complete, atomic marker and **must not be filled with content**. It serves strictly as a field separator.
    *   **Incorrect Example:** `entity<|#|>Tokyo<|location|>Tokyo is the capital of Japan.`
    *   **Correct Example:** `entity<|#|>Tokyo<|#|>location<|#|>Tokyo is the capital of Japan.`

4.  **Relationship Direction & Duplication:**
    *   Treat all relationships as **undirected** unless explicitly stated otherwise. Swapping the source and target entities for an undirected relationship does not constitute a new relationship.
    *   Avoid outputting duplicate relationships.

5.  **Output Order & Prioritization:**
    *   Output all extracted entities first, followed by all extracted relationships.
    *   Within the list of relationships, prioritize and output those relationships that are **most significant** to the core meaning of the input text first.

6.  **Context & Objectivity:**
    *   Ensure all entity names and descriptions are written in the **third person**.
    *   Explicitly name the subject or object; **avoid using pronouns** such as `this article`, `this paper`, `our company`, `I`, `you`, and `he/she`.

Prediabetes is a metabolic condition characterized by elevated blood glucose levels that are higher than normal but not high enough to meet the diagnostic criteria for type 2 diabetes. It is identified through clinical tests such as hemoglobin A1C, fasting plasma glucose (FPG), or oral glucose tolerance testing (OGTT). Specifically, prediabetes is defined by an A1C level between 5.7% and 6.4%, impaired fasting glucose, or impaired glucose tolerance, all of which indicate abnormal glucose metabolism.

This condition serves as a critical precursor to type 2 diabetes, signaling a significantly increased risk for disease progression. Individuals with prediabetes are also at heightened risk for developing cardiovascular complications. The condition is particularly prevalent among certain high-risk populations, including reproductive-age individuals, those with a history of gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM), and people living with HIV, for whom lifelong screening is recommended.

Prediabetes is often asymptomatic but represents a vital window for intervention. Management strategies include lifestyle modifications and, increasingly, the use of digital health technologies combined with online coaching to support behavior change and delay or prevent the onset of type 2 diabetes. Early detection and proactive management are essential to reducing long-term health risks associated with this condition.

A1C, also known as glycated hemoglobin, is a blood test that measures average blood glucose levels over the past 2–3 months and serves as a key clinical indicator of long-term glycemic control. It is widely used in the management and monitoring of diabetes, reflecting average plasma glucose concentrations and providing a reliable assessment of blood glucose trends over time. A1C levels are utilized as primary or secondary outcomes in diabetes research and clinical trials, with structured diabetes training and pump therapy shown to significantly reduce A1C levels compared to control groups or multiple daily insulin injections (MDI), respectively.

The test plays a critical role in the diagnosis and screening of diabetes and prediabetes. An A1C level of 6.5% or higher, measured using NGSP-certified methods, is a diagnostic criterion for diabetes, while levels between 5.9% and 6.4% (41–47 mmol/mol) indicate an increased risk for developing diabetes or prediabetes. It is also used to screen for type 2 diabetes and to identify individuals at high risk for post-transplant diabetes mellitus (PTDM), often in conjunction with fasting glucose measurements. Additionally, A1C levels can rise before the onset of clinical diabetes, making it a useful biomarker for early detection of abnormal glucose metabolism.

However, the utility of A1C varies across specific conditions. It is not recommended for screening cystic fibrosis–related diabetes due to low sensitivity, nor is it reliable for gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) screening after 15 weeks of gestation. Although A1C testing during 24–28 weeks of pregnancy has been evaluated as a potential GDM screening tool, it demonstrates lower effectiveness compared to glucose tolerance tests (GLT). Despite these limitations, A1C remains a cornerstone in diabetes care, providing essential insights into long-term glucose control, disease risk, and treatment efficacy.

Diabetes is a chronic metabolic disorder characterized by elevated blood glucose levels, resulting from the body's inability to produce sufficient insulin, effectively utilize insulin, or both. This condition disrupts carbohydrate metabolism and can lead to glycosuria, with long-term complications affecting vital organs such as the eyes, kidneys, heart, and nervous system. The disease encompasses several types, including type 1 diabetes, which involves the loss of beta-cell mass and function, type 2 diabetes—associated with insulin resistance, lifestyle factors, and the most prevalent form—and rarer forms such as latent autoimmune diabetes in adults. Diagnosis is typically confirmed through clinical tests including A1C, fasting plasma glucose (FPG), or 2-hour plasma glucose (2-h PG) measurements. Effective management requires continuous monitoring of blood glucose levels, adherence to treatment protocols, and often insulin therapy, particularly in cases of severe insulin resistance such as in patients with lipodystrophy, where diabetes frequently emerges during puberty.

The condition demands lifelong medical attention to prevent microvascular and macrovascular complications. Glycemic control has been shown to significantly improve patient outcomes, as demonstrated by long-term studies like the Diabetes Control and Complications Trial/Epidemiology of Diabetes Interventions and Complications (DCCT/EDIC). Research continues to advance understanding of metabolic dysregulation in diabetes, including its development in individuals with HIV due to antiretroviral therapies. Early screening, particularly for type 2 diabetes, is emphasized to enable timely intervention and improve prognosis. Treatment tools such as insulin pens and glucose testing devices are essential but require careful handling and disposal due to the hazardous waste they generate.

In addition to the medical condition, "Diabetes" is also the name of a prominent peer-reviewed scientific journal that plays a central role in advancing research on the disease. The journal has published foundational work, including the original classification and diagnostic criteria for diabetes mellitus and glucose intolerance, as well as simulation studies on early detection and treatment strategies for type 2 diabetes. This dual significance—both as a widespread metabolic disorder and as a key academic publication—underscores the multifaceted nature of diabetes in clinical medicine and scientific inquiry.

The Oral Glucose Tolerance Test (OGTT) is a diagnostic procedure used to evaluate the body's ability to metabolize glucose, primarily serving as a tool for diagnosing diabetes, prediabetes, and related metabolic conditions. The standard form of the test involves the administration of a 75-g glucose solution, with plasma glucose levels measured 2 hours afterward to assess glucose metabolism. This measurement is critical in determining impaired glucose tolerance and diagnosing both type 2 diabetes and prediabetes, with omission of the test known to result in underdiagnosis.

Beyond general diabetes screening, the OGTT holds specific clinical importance in specialized populations. It is the recommended method for annual screening of cystic fibrosis–related diabetes in individuals aged 10 years and older, and is considered the preferred diagnostic approach for confirming posttransplantation diabetes mellitus. Additionally, the test is commonly used in the diagnosis of gestational diabetes, highlighting its broad utility across different forms of dysglycemia. The OGTT is sometimes compared to Hemoglobin A1c for screening purposes but remains the gold standard in certain clinical contexts due to its sensitivity in detecting early metabolic abnormalities.

It is not pre-existing or overt diabetes but is diagnosed during the second or third trimester, most commonly identified through screening between 24 and 28 weeks of pregnancy. Diagnosis is usually confirmed using glucose tolerance tests, and monitoring during pregnancy often involves HbA1c and other glucose assessments to manage blood sugar levels effectively.

Gestational Diabetes Mellitus affects both maternal and neonatal health outcomes, increasing the risk of complications for both mother and child during pregnancy and delivery. These complications may include preeclampsia, cesarean delivery, macrosomia, neonatal hypoglycemia, and other adverse perinatal outcomes. The condition is associated with significant risks not only during pregnancy but also in the long term, as women with a history of GDM have a higher likelihood of developing type 2 diabetes later in life. Similarly, children born to mothers with GDM may face increased risks of obesity and metabolic disorders in the future.

Gestational Diabetes Mellitus is recognized as a temporary yet clinically significant condition that requires careful monitoring and management to optimize health outcomes. It is primarily detected through routine glucose screening procedures during prenatal care, underscoring the importance of early identification and intervention. While GDM typically resolves after childbirth, its implications extend beyond the pregnancy period, necessitating ongoing health surveillance for both mother and child.

Type 2 diabetes is a chronic metabolic disorder characterized by insulin resistance, in which the body's cells fail to respond effectively to insulin, and a relative deficiency in insulin production due to progressive beta-cell dysfunction in the pancreas. This leads to persistent hyperglycemia, or elevated blood glucose levels, which, if uncontrolled, can result in serious long-term complications affecting the cardiovascular system, kidneys, nerves, and eyes. It accounts for 90–95% of all diabetes cases and is commonly associated with obesity, sedentary lifestyle, age, genetic predisposition, and metabolic syndrome. The condition often develops gradually, is typically preceded by prediabetes, and is increasingly being diagnosed in children, adolescents, and individuals of reproductive age, where it may be undiagnosed and linked to adverse pregnancy outcomes. People with a history of gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) are at heightened risk of developing Type 2 diabetes after delivery.

Type 2 diabetes is a heterogeneous and complex disease involving a spectrum of metabolic abnormalities beyond glucose dysregulation, including inflammation and genetic and environmental stress factors. It is distinct from type 1 diabetes in both pathophysiology and management, as it does not involve autoimmune destruction of beta cells. Screening is recommended for asymptomatic adults with risk factors such as overweight, obesity, family history, or specific ethnic backgrounds, and diagnosis is commonly made using HbA1c levels, although pediatric data supporting this method remain limited. Early detection and intervention, through lifestyle modifications or medications like metformin, can reduce the incidence of the disease and improve long-term health outcomes.

Management of Type 2 diabetes is multifaceted and individualized, typically beginning with lifestyle interventions including diet, exercise, and weight management. These are often supplemented with oral antidiabetic medications, and as the disease progresses, insulin therapy may become necessary due to the progressive decline in beta-cell function. Treatment options include basal insulin, multiple daily insulin injections (MDI), and, in select cases, insulin pump therapy—particularly for patients on MDI who meet specific criteria and can safely operate the device. While insulin pumps are not standard for all individuals with Type 2 diabetes, studies such as OpT2mise have explored their efficacy, and structured education programs are being developed to support their use in both adults and youth. Continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) has shown benefits in reducing A1C levels, especially among those on multiple daily injections, though its impact on hypoglycemia varies. The condition is commonly managed in primary care settings and requires an evolving, comprehensive approach integrating lifestyle, pharmacological, and technological strategies to optimize glycemic control and prevent complications.

Type 1 diabetes is a chronic autoimmune condition characterized by the body's inability to produce insulin due to the immune system attacking and destroying the insulin-producing beta cells in the pancreas. This results in absolute insulin deficiency, leading to impaired regulation of blood glucose levels and necessitating lifelong exogenous insulin therapy for survival. The condition is often marked by a rapid onset and can present with acute complications such as diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) and elevated blood glucose levels, particularly if diagnosis is delayed. Historically, Type 1 diabetes was typically fatal within a year of diagnosis before the discovery of insulin; today, it remains a life-long condition requiring continuous and careful management to prevent both acute and long-term complications.

Type 1 diabetes frequently manifests in children and adolescents but can develop at any age, including in adulthood, where it may be misclassified as type 2 diabetes. It is commonly associated with the presence of islet autoantibodies, which serve as key biomarkers for autoimmune activity and help distinguish it from other forms of diabetes. The condition can occur in both sporadic and familial cases, with the risk of development increasing with the number of detected autoantibodies. In some cases, it may be preceded by a preclinical phase involving autoantibody presence, making screening and early detection critical for timely intervention and prevention of DKA. Latent autoimmune diabetes of adulthood (LADA) is also considered part of the Type 1 diabetes spectrum due to its autoimmune etiology and progressive beta-cell destruction.

Management of Type 1 diabetes centers on intensive insulin therapy, delivered through multiple daily injections or insulin delivery systems such as insulin pumps and automated insulin delivery devices. These are often integrated with continuous glucose monitoring (CGM), which enables real-time tracking of glucose levels, reduces the risk of hypoglycemia, and supports precise insulin dosing. Advances in digital health technologies, including closed-loop systems and real-time sensors, are the focus of ongoing clinical research aimed at improving glycemic control, treatment outcomes, and quality of life. Despite significant progress in treatment modalities, external insulin administration remains essential, as the body cannot produce insulin independently. Effective management relies on structured care, patient education, and technological support to maintain metabolic stability and prevent complications associated with chronic hyperglycemia or hypoglycemia. Ongoing research continues to explore screening methods, autoantibody detection, preventive therapies, and potential disease-modifying interventions.

Hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) is a blood test and clinical biomarker that measures the average level of blood glucose over the past two to three months, serving as a critical tool for assessing long-term glycemic control in individuals with diabetes. It reflects the degree to which glucose has become chemically bonded to hemoglobin in red blood cells, forming glycated hemoglobin, a process that occurs gradually and continuously in proportion to blood glucose concentration. Because red blood cells typically survive for about 120 days, the HbA1c level provides a stable and integrated measure of glucose exposure during this period, making it more reliable than daily glucose monitoring, which can be affected by short-term fluctuations.

Hemoglobin A1c is widely used in both clinical practice and research for the diagnosis, screening, and ongoing management of diabetes. It plays a central role in diagnosing type 2 diabetes and prediabetes in adults and children, with an HbA1c level of 6.5% or higher generally indicating diabetes, while levels between 5.7% and 6.4% suggest prediabetes. For individuals already diagnosed with diabetes, HbA1c is a key metric for evaluating the effectiveness of treatment strategies, including medication, diet, and lifestyle changes. A commonly recommended target for most adults is an HbA1c level below 7%, though individualized goals may vary based on factors such as age, comorbidities, and risk of hypoglycemia.

Elevated HbA1c levels are strongly associated with an increased risk of long-term diabetes complications, including neuropathy, retinopathy, nephropathy, and cardiovascular disease. The test does not require fasting, enhancing its convenience and utility in routine care. Additionally, advancements such as continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) have been shown to support improved glycemic outcomes, including reductions in HbA1c, by enabling real-time adjustments to therapy. As a cornerstone of diabetes management, Hemoglobin A1c remains an indispensable tool for guiding clinical decisions and improving patient outcomes.

    *   **Identification:** Identify clearly defined and meaningful entities in the input text.
    *   **Entity Details:** For each identified entity, extract the following information:
        *   `entity_name`: The name of the entity. If the entity name is case-insensitive, capitalize the first letter of each significant word (title case). Ensure **consistent naming** across the entire extraction process.
        *   `entity_type`: Categorize the entity using one of the following types: `Person,Creature,Organization,Location,Event,Concept,Method,Content,Data,Artifact,NaturalObject`. If none of the provided entity types apply, do not add new entity type and classify it as `Other`.
        *   `entity_description`: Provide a concise yet comprehensive description of the entity's attributes and activities, based *solely* on the information present in the input text.
    *   **Output Format - Entities:** Output a total of 4 fields for each entity, delimited by `<|#|>`, on a single line. The first field *must* be the literal string `entity`.
        *   Format: `entity<|#|>entity_name<|#|>entity_type<|#|>entity_description`

2.  **Relationship Extraction & Output:**
    *   **Identification:** Identify direct, clearly stated, and meaningful relationships between previously extracted entities.
    *   **N-ary Relationship Decomposition:** If a single statement describes a relationship involving more than two entities (an N-ary relationship), decompose it into multiple binary (two-entity) relationship pairs for separate description.
        *   **Example:** For "Alice, Bob, and Carol collaborated on Project X," extract binary relationships such as "Alice collaborated with Project X," "Bob collaborated with Project X," and "Carol collaborated with Project X," or "Alice collaborated with Bob," based on the most reasonable binary interpretations.
    *   **Relationship Details:** For each binary relationship, extract the following fields:
        *   `source_entity`: The name of the source entity. Ensure **consistent naming** with entity extraction. Capitalize the first letter of each significant word (title case) if the name is case-insensitive.
        *   `target_entity`: The name of the target entity. Ensure **consistent naming** with entity extraction. Capitalize the first letter of each significant word (title case) if the name is case-insensitive.
        *   `relationship_keywords`: One or more high-level keywords summarizing the overarching nature, concepts, or themes of the relationship. Multiple keywords within this field must be separated by a comma `,`. **DO NOT use `<|#|>` for separating multiple keywords within this field.**
        *   `relationship_description`: A concise explanation of the nature of the relationship between the source and target entities, providing a clear rationale for their connection.
    *   **Output Format - Relationships:** Output a total of 5 fields for each relationship, delimited by `<|#|>`, on a single line. The first field *must* be the literal string `relation`.
        *   Format: `relation<|#|>source_entity<|#|>target_entity<|#|>relationship_keywords<|#|>relationship_description`

3.  **Delimiter Usage Protocol:**
    *   The `<|#|>` is a complete, atomic marker and **must not be filled with content**. It serves strictly as a field separator.
    *   **Incorrect Example:** `entity<|#|>Tokyo<|location|>Tokyo is the capital of Japan.`
    *   **Correct Example:** `entity<|#|>Tokyo<|#|>location<|#|>Tokyo is the capital of Japan.`

4.  **Relationship Direction & Duplication:**
    *   Treat all relationships as **undirected** unless explicitly stated otherwise. Swapping the source and target entities for an undirected relationship does not constitute a new relationship.
    *   Avoid outputting duplicate relationships.

5.  **Output Order & Prioritization:**
    *   Output all extracted entities first, followed by all extracted relationships.
    *   Within the list of relationships, prioritize and output those relationships that are **most significant** to the core meaning of the input text first.

6.  **Context & Objectivity:**
    *   Ensure all entity names and descriptions are written in the **third person**.
    *   Explicitly name the subject or object; **avoid using pronouns** such as `this article`, `this paper`, `our company`, `I`, `you`, and `he/she`.

7.  **Language & Proper Nouns:**
    *   The entire output (entity names, keywords, and descriptions) must be written in `English`.
    *   Proper nouns (e.g., personal names, place names, organization names) should be retained in their original language if a proper, widely accepted translation is not available or would cause ambiguity.

8.  **Completion Signal:** Output the literal string `<|COMPLETE|>` only after all entities and relationships, following all criteria, have been completely extracted and outputted.

The detection of autoantibodies such as anti-GAD, anti-IA2, anti-ZnT8, and anti-insulin supports a diagnosis of type 1 diabetes and helps distinguish it from monogenic or secondary forms of diabetes. Conversely, the absence of autoantibodies is a useful indicator in identifying monogenic diabetes, as these immune markers are typically negative in such cases. Therefore, autoantibody testing plays a vital role in the differential diagnosis of diabetes subtypes.

However, the presence of autoantibodies is not entirely exclusive to type 1 diabetes, as rare instances have been reported in other diabetes forms, including monogenic diabetes, complicating interpretation. Additionally, autoantibodies can interfere with laboratory assays, such as insulin antibody testing, potentially limiting their utility in certain diagnostic contexts. Despite these challenges, autoantibodies remain central to the immunological and clinical characterization of autoimmune diabetes, providing essential insights into disease classification and pathogenesis.

It encompasses specific subtypes such as maturity-onset diabetes of the young (MODY) and neonatal diabetes, which typically manifest early in life—often before the age of 25. However, distinguishing characteristics such as the presence of detectable C-peptide levels above 0.6 ng/ml even after five years of diagnosis, absence of diabetes-related autoantibodies, and a strong family history of diabetes across two or three generations can support clinical suspicion of monogenic diabetes.

Diagnosis of Monogenic Diabetes relies on a combination of clinical criteria and genetic testing. It is often suspected in individuals presenting with hyperglycemia at a young age, particularly when accompanied by a familial pattern of inheritance consistent with autosomal dominant transmission. Unlike typical type 1 diabetes, where C-peptide levels are usually undetectable after several years, patients with monogenic forms may retain significant endogenous insulin production. This preservation of beta-cell function underscores the importance of accurate classification, as treatment strategies can differ significantly—some patients may successfully transition from insulin therapy to oral sulfonylureas, especially in cases linked to specific gene mutations such as those in the KCNJ11 or ABCC8 genes.

A1C, also known as glycated hemoglobin, is a blood test that measures average blood glucose levels over the past 2–3 months and serves as a key clinical indicator of long-term glycemic control. It reflects average plasma glucose concentrations and is widely used in the diagnosis, screening, and management of diabetes and prediabetes. An A1C level of 6.5% or higher, measured using NGSP-certified methods, is a diagnostic criterion for diabetes, while levels between 5.9% and 6.4% (41–47 mmol/mol) indicate an increased risk for developing diabetes or prediabetes. The test is particularly valuable because A1C levels can rise before the onset of clinical diabetes, making it a useful biomarker for early detection of abnormal glucose metabolism and for predicting future diabetes risk.

A1C plays a central role in both clinical practice and research, serving as a primary or secondary outcome in diabetes studies. It is used to monitor treatment efficacy, with interventions such as structured diabetes training and insulin pump therapy shown to significantly reduce A1C levels compared to control groups or multiple daily insulin injections. The test is also employed to screen for type 2 diabetes and to identify individuals at high risk for post-transplant diabetes mellitus (PTDM), often in conjunction with fasting glucose measurements. Despite its broad utility, A1C has limitations in specific populations. It is not recommended for screening cystic fibrosis–related diabetes due to low sensitivity, and it is not reliable for diagnosing gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) after 15 weeks of gestation. Although A1C testing during 24–28 weeks of pregnancy has been evaluated as a potential GDM screening tool, it is less effective than glucose tolerance tests (GLT). Nonetheless, A1C remains a cornerstone in diabetes care, providing essential insights into long-term glucose control, disease risk, and therapeutic outcomes.

Gestational Diabetes Mellitus (GDM) is a form of diabetes that develops during pregnancy, characterized by glucose intolerance or elevated blood glucose levels first recognized during gestation. It is not pre-existing or overt diabetes but is typically diagnosed in the second or third trimester, most commonly between 24 and 28 weeks of pregnancy. Screening for GDM is a routine component of prenatal care and is usually conducted through glucose tolerance tests, with additional monitoring involving HbA1c and other glucose assessments to manage blood sugar levels effectively.

GDM poses significant risks to both maternal and neonatal health. Maternal complications may include preeclampsia and an increased likelihood of cesarean delivery, while fetal and neonatal risks encompass macrosomia, neonatal hypoglycemia, and other adverse perinatal outcomes. Although GDM generally resolves after childbirth, it has important long-term health implications. Women with a history of GDM face a substantially higher risk of developing type 2 diabetes later in life, and their children are at increased risk for obesity and metabolic disorders. As such, GDM is considered a temporary yet clinically significant condition requiring careful management during pregnancy and ongoing health surveillance for both mother and child beyond delivery. Early identification through routine glucose screening is critical to optimizing health outcomes.

The Carpenter-Coustan Criteria are a set of diagnostic guidelines used to identify gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) through the interpretation of a 100-gram oral glucose tolerance test (100-g OGTT). These criteria are specifically applied in the two-step approach to GDM diagnosis, which begins with an initial 50-gram glucose screen; if this screening yields a positive result, the 100-g OGTT is administered and its results are evaluated using the Carpenter-Coustan thresholds.

The Carpenter-Coustan Criteria define specific glucose threshold values for fasting, 1-hour, 2-hour, and 3-hour measurements during the 100-g OGTT. A diagnosis of GDM is confirmed when at least two of these glucose values exceed the established thresholds. This method provides a standardized framework for diagnosing GDM, ensuring consistency in clinical assessment and enabling timely intervention to manage maternal and fetal health risks associated with abnormal glucose metabolism during pregnancy.

Type 2 Diabetes is a chronic metabolic disorder characterized by insulin resistance, in which the body's cells fail to respond effectively to insulin, and a relative deficiency in insulin production due to progressive beta-cell dysfunction in the pancreas. This leads to persistent hyperglycemia, or elevated blood glucose levels, which, if uncontrolled, can result in serious long-term complications affecting the cardiovascular system, kidneys, nerves, and eyes. It accounts for 90–95% of all diabetes cases and is distinct from type 1 diabetes, as it does not involve autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells. The condition is commonly associated with obesity, sedentary lifestyle, age, genetic predisposition, metabolic syndrome, and specific ethnic backgrounds. It often develops gradually, is typically preceded by prediabetes, and is increasingly being diagnosed in children, adolescents, and individuals of reproductive age, where it may remain undiagnosed and contribute to adverse pregnancy outcomes. Individuals with a history of gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) are at heightened risk of developing Type 2 Diabetes after delivery.

The pathophysiology of Type 2 Diabetes is heterogeneous and complex, involving a spectrum of metabolic abnormalities beyond glucose dysregulation, including chronic inflammation, genetic factors, and environmental stress. Diagnosis is commonly made using HbA1c levels, although the use of this criterion in pediatric populations remains limited by insufficient data. Screening is recommended for asymptomatic adults with risk factors such as overweight, obesity, or family history, and early detection through such screening can enable interventions that reduce the incidence of the disease. Lifestyle modifications, including diet, exercise, and weight management, along with medications such as metformin, have been shown to delay or prevent the onset of Type 2 Diabetes and improve long-term health outcomes.

Management of Type 2 Diabetes is multifaceted and individualized, typically beginning with lifestyle interventions and often progressing to oral antidiabetic medications. As beta-cell function declines over time, insulin therapy—such as basal insulin, multiple daily injections (MDI), or, in select cases, insulin pump therapy—may become necessary. While insulin pumps are not standard for all patients, studies like OpT2mise have explored their efficacy, particularly in those already on MDI, and structured education programs are being developed to support their use in both adults and youth. Continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) has demonstrated benefits in lowering A1C levels, especially among individuals on multiple daily injections, though its effects on hypoglycemia vary. The condition is commonly managed in primary care and requires an evolving, comprehensive approach integrating lifestyle, pharmacological, and technological strategies to optimize glycemic control and prevent complications.

Type 1 diabetes is a chronic autoimmune condition characterized by the immune system's destruction of insulin-producing beta cells in the pancreas, leading to absolute insulin deficiency. This results in the body's inability to regulate blood glucose levels, necessitating lifelong exogenous insulin therapy for survival. The condition often presents with a rapid onset and can lead to acute complications such as diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) and significantly elevated blood glucose levels, particularly if diagnosis is delayed. Historically fatal within a year of diagnosis before the discovery of insulin, Type 1 diabetes now requires continuous, intensive management to prevent both acute and long-term complications.

Although commonly diagnosed in children and adolescents, Type 1 diabetes can develop at any age, including in adults over 30, where it is frequently misclassified as type 2 diabetes. This misclassification underscores the importance of accurate diagnostic criteria, particularly the detection of islet autoantibodies, which are key biomarkers of autoimmune activity and help differentiate Type 1 diabetes from other forms. The presence of multiple autoantibodies increases the risk of developing the condition and may precede clinical onset during a preclinical phase, making autoantibody screening critical for early detection and intervention to prevent DKA. Latent autoimmune diabetes of adulthood (LADA) is recognized as part of the Type 1 diabetes spectrum due to its autoimmune etiology and progressive beta-cell destruction.

Management of Type 1 diabetes centers on intensive insulin therapy, delivered via multiple daily injections or insulin delivery systems such as insulin pumps and automated insulin delivery devices. These are increasingly integrated with continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) to enable real-time glucose tracking, reduce hypoglycemia risk, and support precise insulin dosing. Advances in digital health technologies, including closed-loop systems, are the focus of ongoing research aimed at improving glycemic control and quality of life. Despite these innovations, exogenous insulin remains essential, as endogenous insulin production is absent. Ongoing research continues to explore screening strategies, preventive therapies, and potential disease-modifying interventions to alter the course of this lifelong condition.

The sensor collects glucose data at regular intervals—typically every few minutes, often as frequently as every 5 minutes—providing real-time, dynamic insights into glucose trends, fluctuations, and patterns throughout the day and night. This allows individuals, particularly those with type 1 diabetes or type 2 diabetes requiring insulin therapy, to make timely adjustments to insulin dosing, diet, or physical activity, thereby improving glycemic outcomes and reducing the risk of complications.

Many systems include real-time alerts for rapid glucose changes or values outside preset thresholds, facilitating proactive interventions. Clinical guidelines increasingly recommend CGM for individuals on insulin therapy due to its demonstrated benefits in reducing hypoglycemia and improving overall glucose control. The technology is also utilized in retrospective analysis and virtual or hospital-based clinical settings, where continuous data supports informed treatment decisions and improved patient outcomes.

Beyond general diabetes care, Continuous Glucose Monitoring has been discussed in international consensus statements and studied for specialized applications. For instance, CGM may be more sensitive than the oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) in detecting early risk for progression to cystic fibrosis–related diabetes, although it is not currently recommended for routine screening in this context. Additionally, CGM data can be compared with A1C measurements to provide a more complete picture of long-term and daily glucose control, bridging the gap between laboratory results and real-time monitoring. As a transformative advancement in diabetes management, CGM supports safer, more informed, and personalized care, representing a significant evolution from traditional blood glucose monitoring methods.
